summary: Describes Tree Engineering for Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER-TE), which steers BIER multicast packets along strict or loose paths without per-flow state in the network. It gives the bit positions in the packet a new meaning, so they indicate adjacencies rather than destinations, and it serves as the path steering mechanism for traffic engineering with BIER. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: BIER marks which receivers should get a copy. This version instead marks which roads to use, so a sender can plan exactly how the copies spread out.

questions: how does bier traffic engineering work
how does bier-te forward multicast packets
what does the donotclear flag do in bier-te
how does bier-te save bit positions
subtitle: BIER multicast where the bits in the packet name the links to cross, so a controller can steer each copy along an exact tree.

tldr.problem: BIER sends multicast packets to a set of egress routers, but the network's routing decides the paths. Operators who need strict or loose path steering have no way to say which links a multicast tree must use.
tldr.mechanism: BIER-TE gives the bit positions in the packet a new meaning: each bit stands for an adjacency (a link or hop) in the BIER-TE topology instead of for an egress router. A controller fills each router's forwarding table and builds the BitString that lists the edges of the desired loop-free tree.
tldr.outcome: Routers stay stateless per packet and need no BIER routing underlay for most adjacencies. The price is that bits are scarcer, so the controller must save bit positions and avoid loops and duplicates.

today: RFC 9262 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2022. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 8279 and RFC 8296, and it has no IANA actions.

sections.title: BIER-TE in Brief
sections.content:
Tree Engineering for Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER-TE) builds on the BIER architecture of RFC 8279 and the packet formats of RFC 8296. The RFC expects the reader to know both. It describes per-packet stateless strict and loose path-steered replication and forwarding, and it is meant as the path steering mechanism for Traffic Engineering with BIER.

The core change is the meaning of a bit position (BP). In BIER, a BP in the packet's BitString indicates a Bit-Forwarding Egress Router (BFER). In BIER-TE, a BP indicates an adjacency of the network topology, so the packet's BitString lists the edges of a loop-free tree. Each router's Bit Index Forwarding Table (BIFT) holds only the BPs that are adjacent to it. A router replicates the packet to every adjacency whose bit is set, and normally clears those bits as it forwards.

BIER-TE can reuse BIER forwarding engines with little or no change, and it can live in the same domain as BIER, for example in separate BIER subdomains. Except for optional routed adjacencies, it needs no BIER routing underlay, so it can run without an IGP.
sections.plainLanguage: Normal BIER says who should get a copy. BIER-TE says which roads the copies must drive on. A planner called the controller picks the roads ahead of time.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Figure 1 of the RFC shows six routers, BFR1 to BFR6, with bit positions p1 to p15. Each router's table maps a few bits to either forward_connected() (send to a directly connected neighbor) or local_decap() (take the packet off the network and hand the payload up).

To send a packet from BFR1 via BFR4 to BFR6, the BitString is (p2,p8,p10,p12,p15). On BFR1 the only bit also present in its table is p2, so BFR1 sends the single copy to BFR2. BFR2 forwards to BFR4 because of p8, BFR4 to BFR5 because of p10, and BFR5 to BFR6 because of p12. Finally p15 makes BFR6 decapsulate the packet.

Changing one bit changes the path. Using p6 instead of p5 makes BFR5 rather than BFR2 copy the packet towards BFR3. The topology lets traffic cross any possible path and be replicated where desired.

A second example replaces some routers with plain unicast routers (Rtr2 and Rtr5). The adjacencies across them are called forward_routed(), and BFR1 can reach BFR6 via BFR3 with the BitString (p1,p5,p9).
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a treasure map where each stamp on the ticket is one road. A road only works at the crossroads that know that stamp. Stamp the ticket with the right roads and it follows your route.

sections.title: Components and the Controller
sections.content:
BIER-TE has the same three layers as BIER: the multicast flow overlay, the BIER layer, and the routing underlay. The BIER layer splits into the BIER-TE forwarding plane and the BIER-TE control plane. The reference control plane is a single, centralized BIER-TE controller, though an operator could also configure BFRs by CLI, or the control plane could be distributed.

The controller decides the BIER-TE topology (which adjacencies get which bit positions), derives each BFR's BIFT by extracting that router's adjacencies, installs the tables, and computes the BitStrings that the ingress routers (BFIRs) impose. Talking to routers can use standardized protocols such as NETCONF, RESTCONF, YANG or PCEP, or a vendor CLI. In statically managed networks, such as industrial environments, topology discovery and creation can be manual and offline.

In BIER the same set of egress routers always gives the same BitString. In BIER-TE the BitString encodes paths, so it differs by ingress router and by policy: shortest path trees, Steiner trees (minimum cost trees), diverse path trees for redundancy, and so on.

On failures, BIER-TE can use Fast Reroute procedures (described elsewhere) or more slowly have the controller recompute and push new BitStrings.
sections.plainLanguage: A planner in a control room draws the route for each delivery and gives every sender the right ticket. If a road breaks, either a quick local detour is used or the planner issues new tickets.

sections.title: The Bit Index Forwarding Table
sections.content:
The BIER-TE BIFT is equivalent to the BIER one and exists on every router running BIER-TE, per subdomain. Rows are indexed by BIFT-index = SI * BSL + BP - 1, where SI is the Set Identifier, BSL the BitString length, and BPs are numbered from 1 to BSL. The RFC also writes this as SI:BP. The minimum BSL supported by BIER and BIER-TE is 64.

In BIER, each row points to the next hop towards one egress router. In BIER-TE, a row identifies one adjacency, or several if the bit is reused, and is filled in only on the router upstream of that adjacency. Other routers leave the row empty. A BP may be populated on more than one router to save bits.

The TE topology can be drawn as a directed graph whose edges are adjacencies labeled with BPs. A topology of connected adjacencies is called an underlay topology, one of only routed adjacencies an overlay topology, and a mix a hybrid topology.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router keeps a short list saying 'if the ticket has stamp 5, send a copy down this road.' Stamps that are not its own are simply ignored.

sections.title: Adjacency Types
sections.content:
A bit in the BIFT can point to one of four kinds of adjacency.

  • forward_connected() goes to a directly connected neighbor and is only layer 2 forwarded, not routed. It can carry a DoNotClear (DNC) flag, which keeps the bit set in the copy sent on that adjacency. Only this adjacency type may use DNC.
  • forward_routed() uses a tunneling encapsulation (for example MPLS or IP/GRE) so the routing underlay carries the packet to an l3-neighbor. It crosses routers that do not support BIER-TE.
  • ECMP() lists two or more non-ECMP adjacencies and an optional seed, and a hash picks one. If the packet has an entropy field, the same entropy value SHOULD go to the same adjacency.
  • local_decap() removes the BIER header and passes the payload to the protocol in the router, which makes it a BFER for those packets.

BFRs MUST support forward_connected() without DNC, forward_routed() and local_decap(), with zero or one adjacency per bit. They SHOULD support DNC and more than one adjacency on a bit. ECMP() is a MAY.
sections.plainLanguage: A stamp can mean 'walk next door,' 'take a taxi past the roads that do not know our stamps,' 'pick any one of these equal roads,' or 'stop here and open the package.'

sections.title: Forwarding Rules
sections.content:
When a packet arrives, the router looks up each set bit of the BitString in its BIFT. For every bit that has an adjacency, it makes a copy as that adjacency requires. Before sending, it clears all BPs in the packet for which it has an adjacency, which stops packets looping even if a BitString erroneously contains a loop. A DNC adjacency is the exception: its own bit is set again in the copy sent over it.

The forwarding pseudocode is based on the BIER pseudocode of RFC 8279 with one change. BIER clears the forwarded bits from the original packet after the first copy, and that step must not be done for BIER-TE. Bit clearing is done through the Forwarding Bit Mask of each row. A second, fuller version of the pseudocode drops the per-bit masks and supports DNC, several adjacencies per bit and ECMP().

Encapsulation is outside the scope of the document, but the RFC explains that a router must tell BIER and BIER-TE packets apart. With the BIER encapsulation, the BIFT-id field can do that, and the BIFT-id space can be shared between BIER and BIER-TE BIFTs.
sections.plainLanguage: At each crossroads you tear off the stamps that belong to that crossroads before sending copies on. That way a ticket cannot send copies in circles forever.

sections.title: Saving Bit Positions
sections.content:
The BitString size limits the domain, so Section 5 of the RFC lists tricks for using fewer bits.

  • P2P links: one BP serves both routers on the link.
  • Leaf BFERs: leaf egress routers addressed by the same BitString can share one local_decap() BP.
  • LANs and hub and spoke: one BP can carry a list of forward_connected() adjacencies when copies to all neighbors are acceptable, but redundantly connected neighbors need their own bits.
  • Rings: setting DNC lets one bit run around a ring; two bits (one per direction) cover entry at any ring router.
  • ECMP(): N parallel choices need one BP instead of N. Using different seeds on consecutive hops avoids polarization, where the same hash always picks the same branch.
  • forward_routed(): tunnels across routers where neither steering nor replication is needed, and allows incremental deployment.
  • Reuse: a BP can repeat across routers that no single path crosses in sequence.

Larger domains use several Set Identifiers and subdomains, and the controller assigns BFR-ids, which BIER-TE forwarding itself does not need.
sections.plainLanguage: Stamps are scarce, so the planner lets one stamp cover several similar roads, or lets a stamp be used in different parts of town where no trip ever needs both.

sections.title: Security and Misconfiguration Risks
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8279 and, when used, RFC 8296 also apply. BIER-TE supports unicast tunneling through forward_routed() adjacencies, so the BIER domain's security model must also filter incoming tunneled packets and stop forward_routed() adjacencies from leaking BIER packets out of the domain.

Controller to router communication is much more commonly secured with SSH or TLS than IGPs are, and BIER-TE controllers SHOULD use security equal to or better than those mechanisms.

The RFC names misconfiguration as the most important attack vector. DNC entries could create persistent loops that end only because of TTL. To limit this, DNC is allowed only on forward_connected() adjacencies and relies on port-unique link layer addresses, and clearing of adjacency bits is as strict as possible. The controller must also ensure BitStrings form trees, since a BitString that redundantly connects routers causes duplicates.
sections.plainLanguage: The biggest danger is a mistake in the map or tickets, like a road wired back onto itself. The stamp rules keep a mistake from making an endless pile of copies.

items.label: Connected neighbor
items.desc: Layer 2 forwarding to a directly connected BFR; may set DNC.

items.label: Routed neighbor
items.desc: Tunnels the packet via the routing underlay to an l3-neighbor.

items.label: Equal-cost choice
items.desc: Hash picks one of two or more adjacencies; optional seed.

items.label: Local decapsulation
items.desc: Passes the payload to the protocol in the router; makes it a BFER.
